analysis.investment_thesis: Indigo Paints is a decent but capital-hungry challenger in a good industry, permanently fighting uphill against Asian Paints, Berger, and Nerolac which possess far superior scale, distribution, and brand moats. At 26.9x earnings with revenue growth decelerating to 2.7% and net profit actually falling in FY2025, the price is fair at best — not compelling enough for a new position.
key_strengths: Virtually debt-free balance sheet (D/E: 0.02) with clean, consistent operating cash flows — 4/4 years positive
ROCE of 19.5% and gross margin of 45.7% suggest reasonable pricing power in specialty segments (floor coatings, metallic emulsions)
Strong 3-year earnings CAGR of 19.1% and FCF turning meaningfully positive (₹70 Cr in FY2025) show improving capital efficiency
key_risks: Shareholder in a tough neighborhood: Asian Paints, Berger, and Nerolac have 5-10x the scale, brand depth, and dealer networks — Indigo's moat is narrow and contested
FY2025 growth stalled badly — revenue grew just 2.7% (₹1,306→₹1,341 Cr) and net profit declined ₹149→₹142 Cr, suggesting pricing pressure and volume headwinds
Capital intensity remains high: ₹221 Cr CWIP in FY2025 signals another heavy capex cycle ahead, which historically has suppressed FCF and returns on equity
red_flags: FY2025 net profit contraction despite revenue growth — a warning sign of margin compression
ROE of 14.6% falls below my 15% minimum threshold; particularly disappointing for a business that has been investing heavily for years
Competing directly with Asian Paints is like fighting Coca-Cola with a regional soda brand — the entrenched giants' distribution moats are very hard to dislodge
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Indigo Paints operates in a structurally attractive industry — decorative paints in India benefit from premiumization, real estate cycles, and sticky brand preferences. However, attractiveness of the industry does not confer attractiveness on every participant. Indigo is the #4 player by revenue, and in consumer-facing branded businesses, being #4 in a market dominated by giants like Asian Paints (which I consider one of the finest businesses in India) is a difficult strategic position. Their differentiation via specialty products is real but replicable, and the Big Three have the distribution reach to copy any product innovation.

The financials tell a mixed story. The balance sheet is admirably clean (D/E: 0.02), and the 3-year earnings trajectory looked promising. But FY2025 is concerning: revenue effectively flatlined at ₹1,341 Cr (+2.7%), net profit slipped to ₹142 Cr from ₹149 Cr, and the ₹221 Cr CWIP signals another capex-heavy phase ahead. FCF of ₹70 Cr is modest relative to a ₹4,000 Cr market cap — that's a ~1.75% FCF yield, which is thin. At 26.9x trailing earnings with decelerating growth and a sub-15% ROE, I'm simply not getting a sufficient margin of safety. I'd want to see sustained 20%+ earnings growth, expanding ROE above 18%, and evidence that the moat is widening before paying this price.
